*   Determine the parameter $t \in [0, 1]$ along the segment $f(u)f(v)$ such that $w = (1-t)f(u) + t f(v)$ [S1].

The claim states that one must determine the parameter $t$ along the segment $f(u)f(v)$ such that $w = (1-t)f(u) + t f(v)$. The evidence in Source [S1], specifically within the description of Algorithm 1 and the text describing Stage III/IV, explicitly mentions: 'Find parameter t on f (u) f (v) for w' and 'Interpolate vertex e = u + t(v − u)'. The formula $e = u + t(v - u)$ is mathematically equivalent to $w = (1-t)f(u) + t f(v)$ if we consider the interpolation of the position in the domain corresponding to the intersection point $w$ in the range, or more accurately, the text implies finding $t$ such that the point on the segment in the range is $w$, and using that same $t$ to interpolate the domain vertex. The specific notation $w = (1-t)f(u) + t f(v)$ represents the linear interpolation of the range values $f(u)$ and $f(v)$ to find the intersection point $w$. The evidence supports finding this parameter $t$ for the intersection $w$ on the segment $f(u)f(v)$.

Fiber Surface Extraction generalizes isosurface extraction from univariate scalar fields to bivariate vector fields by extracting the preimage of a curve in the range space [S1].

The claim states that Fiber Surface Extraction generalizes isosurface extraction from univariate scalar fields to bivariate vector fields by extracting the preimage of a curve in the range space. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this: Section 5 defines fiber surfaces for lines (a type of curve) in the range as isosurfaces of a derived scalar field (generalizing the concept). Section 6 extends this to arbitrary curves (polygons) in the range, defining the fiber surface as the preimage $f^{-1}(P)$ of a polygon $P$ in the range space. The algorithm described (Algorithm 1) extracts this surface by adapting Marching Cubes (an isosurface extraction algorithm) to handle the preimage of the curve in the range, thus confirming the generalization from univariate isosurfaces to bivariate vector field preimages of curves.
